info.bio:
Steven Patrick Morrissey nació el 22 de mayo de 1959 en Davyhulme, Manchester, Inglaterra. Desde muy temprana edad se sintió atraído por la escritura, dándole prioridad a la poesía. Sus principales influencias van desde Oscar Wilde a Goethe, además de ser fanático de la música pop y el cine.

En 1980, Morrissey conoce al guitarrista Johnny Marr, quien lo invitó a colaborar con él. Luego incluyeron a otros compañeros de Marr, el bajista Andy Rourke y el baterista Mike Joyce

scenes.name: Cantautores de los ochenta
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Absorbida la new wave, el mundo de los cantautores no vuelve a ser el mismo: los referentes pasan a ser Dylan, Neil Young, Cohen, Tim Buckley y Joni Mitchell. Las mujeres recuperan su estatus de seres filosóficos: Phranc, Suzanne Vega, Tracy Chapman, Melissa Etheridge, Michelle Shocked, Barbara Manning, Lucinda y Victoria Williams, Indigo Girls y, en Canadá, Jane Siberry, Mary Margaret O'Hara y Sarah McLachlan. Excéntricos: Jandek, Daniel Johnston, David Thomas, Alejandro Escovedo; en California, Stan Ridgway, Chris Isaak y Smog. En Gran Bretaña, Billy Bragg, Robyn Hitchcock, Julian Cope y, la voz más importante de la década, Nick Cave, predicador del apocalipsis moral (From Her To Eternity, The Good Son). Sinéad O'Connor, Sting, Morrissey, Momus; el pop celta de Enya y Loreena McKennitt; al cambiar la década, Joe Henry, Daniel Lanois y Bob Mould.

podcast.body: Mick Ronson, who produced for Morrissey, died in April 1993 from cancer. "Mick Ronson, David Bowie's guitarist and Morrissey's producer, Cancer April 1993."

podcast.title: Records Banned by Spillers Records (2019)
podcast.body: In 2019, Spillers Records, a long-standing record store in Cardiff, Wales, banned all of Morrissey's records from its inventory. This decision was made because the store's management believed Morrissey was aligning too closely with far-right politics and groups. "In 2019, they banned all of his records because they believe Maserah is floating too much with far-right politics and far-right groups."

podcast.title: Backstage Rider – Festival Meat Preparation Buffer
podcast.body: When performing at festivals with other acts, Morrissey's rider politely requests that his dressing rooms be situated away from any barbecued or meat preparation areas, and not downwind, to avoid the aroma of cooking meat reaching him or the band. "The performer politely requests that where barbecued food meat is being prepared, that the Moorse dressing rooms are situated away from any meat preparation and not downwind."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Backstage Rider – Personal Food Preferences
podcast.body: Morrissey's rider typically requests salt and vinegar chips, a bottle of red wine, cornflakes, Coco-Puffs or Special K, a pint of milk, two green apples, a packet of cashews, cheese sandwiches, and a cupcake. "Salt and vinegar chips, a bottle of red wine, cornflakes, coca-puffs, or special K, a pint of milk, two green apples, a packet of cashews, cheese sandwiches, and a cupcake."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Backstage Rider – Ticketed Vegan Policy
podcast.body: Tickets for Morrissey's shows often feature an important note stating that "only vegan food options will be available for purchase for this event" and that "outside food containing meat, dairy, or other animal products will not be permitted inside the venue," reinforcing his strict dietary stance. "Important, please note only vegan food options will be available for purchase for this event. Outside food containing meat, dairy, or other animal products will not be permitted inside the venue."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Backstage Rider – Venue-Wide Vegetarianism
podcast.body: Morrissey's rider often includes a controversial clause: if he is performing, everyone in the venue must be vegetarian for that night. This means no meat is to be sold or served anywhere in the venue, with meat treated as a "prohibited item," and this rule is strongly policed. "If Moorse is going to be a vegetarian, then everyone in the venue has to be a vegetarian for that night."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Charisma and Media Appeal
podcast.body: Morrissey, the singer of The Smiths, possessed notable charisma and a strong personality. He was known for being quick with "pithy outrageous quotes," a characteristic that made him particularly popular with the British music media. "He had charisma and personality to burn and he was quick with a pithy outrageous quote."

podcast.title: Controversial Interview Style
podcast.body: Morrissey was known for his confrontational approach in interviews, particularly with sensationalist newspapers like The Sun. He would often make incendiary statements, which further fueled press controversies and scrutiny surrounding The Smiths. "Y digamos que Morrisa y entraba mucho al trapo. Morrisa y decía cosas muy incendiarias en muchas de sus entrevistas que incitaban todavía que las prensas hechas en más encima sobre la banda."

podcast.title: Literary Background
podcast.body: From his adolescence, Morrissey was a dedicated literature enthusiast. He actively wrote poetry, participated in literature clubs, and had even published a book about music and several poems, earning recognition for his literary pursuits during his teenage years. "Morrisa era un gran aficionado a la literatura, ya dolescente, escribía mucho, escribía poesía, estaban clubes de literatura, de hecho, ya había escrito algún libro sobre música y algunos poemas, era bastante reconocido por eso, ya da adolescente."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Lyrical Influences
podcast.body: When starting The Smiths, Morrissey deliberately sought lyrical inspiration from literature rather than relying on previous musical influences, which was the common practice. His key literary inspirations included Oscar Wilde, Walt Whitman, and classic British Victorian novels, shaping his distinct writing style. "cuando empieza el proyecto de los Smith, Morrisa inó busca sus influencias para las letras en la música anterior, como solía pasar, sino que busca sus influencias en la literatura."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: THE SMITHS: Un antes y un después en la forma de componer.

podcast.title: Rediscovery of Joe Brieaz
podcast.body: During his solo tour, Morrissey discovered the music and story of Joe Brieaz and was completely captivated by his material. He attempted to organize fundraising and provide artistic support, unaware that Joe Brieaz had already been deceased for many years. "Morris y durante la gina de solitario de llora Arsenal que descubría la figura de llobria así que ha completamente innotizado por su material y quiso hacer un poco de intentar ayudar a recodar fondos y de ayudarlo como artista sin darse de cuenta de que llobria llevaba ya muchos años muerto."

podcast.title: Royalty Dispute and Appeals
podcast.body: Morrissey was sued by former Smiths bandmates Mike Joyce and Andy Rourke in 1996 for non-payment of royalties. While Andy Rourke settled for £80,000, Mike Joyce was awarded £1.2 million, a decision Morrissey continues to appeal. "Morrissey, by the way, still hasn't paid up because he keeps appealing it to the courts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Social and Geographic References
podcast.body: The album "On Lovin High School" includes multiple thematic references to both "RL" and "Tel Aviv," alongside broader social content. "hay varios temas en los que se hace referencia de RL y a Tel Aviv, etcétera, también se hace referencia al contenido social."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Solo Career Trajectory
podcast.body: After The Smiths' breakup, Morrissey initially seemed poised to become a major solo star, benefiting from the cult following he amassed with his previous band. However, his solo career began to decline in the mid-1990s, as he struggled to produce consistent albums, moved to Los Angeles, refused interviews, and toured less frequently. "Although it got off to a promising start, Morris' solo career hit the skids in the mid 1990s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Successful Solo Foray
podcast.body: Morrissey launched his solo career months after The Smiths disbanded in the fall of 1987. He has continued to make records on his own ever since, establishing himself as one of the more successful solo artists in modern rock history. "Morrissey, one of the more successful solo forays in the history of modern rock."

xref.title: Morrissey Curates Reunion at Meltdown Festival (2004)
xref.body: In 2004, Morrissey was invited to curate England's Meltdown Festival and used this opportunity to fulfill a personal dream by reuniting his favorite band, the New York Dolls. "In 2004, Morrissey was asked to curate a music festival in England called the Meltdown Festival, knowing that this was his opportunity to make a personal dream come true. He made it his mission to reunite his favorite band of all time, and he did."

xref.title: Andy Rourke Death (May 18, 2023) – Pancreatic Cancer, Age 59; Sued Morrissey, Later Played Two Morrissey Singles
xref.body: Andy Rourke was a founding member of the Smiths and is considered by fans one of the greatest bassists in the history of British indie rock. His time with the band ended badly: a heroin addiction, a lawsuit against Morrissey and Johnny Marr for unpaid royalties (he was broke), and a decade later a bankruptcy over tax issues. Post-Smiths, he worked with the Pretenders, Killing Joke, Stone Roses singer Ian Brown, Dolores O'Riordan and the Cranberries, and Peter Hook of New Order. In a remarkable reconciliation, he played on two Morrissey solo singles despite the money disputes. His father and sister were both diagnosed with cancer, which prompted him to start a cancer charity; he himself was later diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. He died in a New York hospital on May 18, 2023, age 59. "Ask any Smiths fan, and they'll tell you that he was one of the greatest bassists in the history of British Indie Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Admiration from Renowned Artists
xref.body: O'Hara garnered significant praise and admiration from many influential musicians; Morrissey requested her for vocalizations on his single "November Spawned a Demon," and Michael Stipe of R.E.M., Radiohead, Bruce Cockburn, Dave Matthews, and Nick Cave were all noted fans of her distinct music. "Moresy was such a fan that he asked her to do some vocalizations on his single November Spawn Demonstrer. Michael Steip couldn't get enough of her. Radiohead, Bruce Coburn, Dave Matthews, Nick Cave, they were all fans."

xref.title: Alex Turner's Lyrical Talent
xref.body: Alex Turner is recognized as one of the best lyricists of his generation in non-hip hop music, possibly one of the best alt-rock lyricists since Morrissey. He developed a habit of writing song lyrics in the back of his school books when bored in high school.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Apology and Resolution
xref.body: In 2019, Morrissey issued an apology for his "terrible things" said about Robert Smith 35 years prior, claiming he "didn't mean them" and jokingly attributing it to Tourette's syndrome (which he does not have). Smith accepted the apology, noting the feud had long faded from his consciousness. "In 2019, Morrissey said, I said some terrible things about him 35 years ago, but I didn't mean them. It's great when you complain everything on Tourette's syndrome."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Band Name Origin
xref.body: The name "The Smiths" was deliberately chosen because Morrissey and Marr couldn't think of anything more plain or boring, making a statement against the fancy names of other Alt Rock bands of the early 80s like Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark and Depeche Mode. It was also a homage to New York poet Patti Smith, one of Morrissey's heroes, and possibly a nod to a 1960s Manchester nightclub called Mr. Smiths. "They chose the name the Smiths because they couldn't think of anything more plain or anything more boring. That was very deliberate."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Commitment to Simple Pop Principles
xref.body: Teaming up with guitarist Johnny Marr, Morrissey formed The Smiths, a band dedicated to simple pop principles, focusing on lyrics that conveyed honest teenage angst or explored darker themes like the murder of real-life kidnapped children. "So, teaming up with guitarist Johnny Marr, they formed a band that was dedicated to simple pop principles. So long's featuring lyrics that really had something to say, be it honest, teenage, angst, or perhaps the murder of real-life kidnap children."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Cult of Personality around Morrissey
xref.body: The Smiths' cult of personality was heavily centered around Stephen Patrick Morrissey, who was perceived as a romantic loner. Fans worshiped him, and he fostered an image of being an outspoken and enigmatic lead singer. "The Smiths Cult of Personality was centered around Stephen Patrick Morrissey, a kid from Manchester, who fancied himself to be a romantic loner."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Empathy for Alienated Fans
xref.body: The Smiths, much like Depeche Mode and The Cure, provided comfort and solace to troubled, sensitive, shy, and alienated music fans. Morrissey's ability to not only understand but also articulate their pain was a key factor in the band's deep connection with its audience. "Morrissey not only understood their pain, but could articulate it like no one else."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence from David Bowie
xref.body: The Smiths, particularly a young Morrissey and Johnny Marr from Manchester, were profoundly influenced by David Bowie, especially his album "Scary Monsters and Super Creeps." Bowie's impact on their formation and sound was so significant that it is suggested modern music, as it is known today, might not exist without his influence on them. "Again, a hugely influential album, especially on a young kid from Manchester named Morrissey and is soon to be mate Johnny Mar. Again, no Bowie, no Smiths."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence from David Bowie's Scary Monsters
xref.body: Both Stephen Patrick Morrissey and Johnny Marr were profoundly influenced by David Bowie's album "Scary Monsters and Super Creeps," to the extent that it's suggested The Smiths would not have existed without Bowie's influence. "No Bowie? No Smiths."

xref.title: Internal Band Conflicts and Disintegration
xref.body: After "The Queen Is Dead," The Smiths faced numerous internal issues, including problems with management. Bass player Andy Rourke was temporarily fired due to a heroin addiction. Johnny Marr was involved in a suspicious car accident on November 12, 1986. Craig Gannon, who had joined as a fifth member, was fired weeks later. Johnny Marr grew tired of Morrissey's dictatorial tendencies, self-centeredness, and public tirades. These factors led to the band's breakup. "Base player Andy Warck was temporarily fired due to a massive heroin addiction. Johnny Marr was nearly killed in a suspicious car accident on November 12, 1986."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Smiths

xref.title: Morrissey's Discontent with 1980s Pop
xref.body: Stephen Patrick Morrissey, a fan of both the New York Dolls and the Sex Pistols, was distressed by what he perceived as the "vacuous state of pop music in the early 1980s," believing it had been hijacked by major record companies. "Stephen Patrick Morrissey was both a fan of the New York Dolls and the Sex Pistols. He was quite distressed at what he considered to be the vacuous state of pop music in the early 1980s. According to Morrissey, music had once again been hijacked by the major record companies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Morrissey's Early Life and Influences
xref.body: In the 1970s, Morrissey devoured music magazines, wrote letters to the editor criticizing critics, and became a big fan of Oscar Wilde, a flamboyant Victorian-era writer known for his love of fresh flowers and controversial lifestyle. Morrissey also worked for the tax department and a hospital morgue before pursuing music. "Morrissey became a big fan of Oscar Wilde, the flamboyant and controversial Victorian era writer who loved fresh flowers and apparently other men, something for which he served two years in prison."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Smiths

xref.title: Morrissey's First Band
xref.body: This group was Morrissey's first serious attempt at a musical endeavor, featuring guitarist Billy Duffy. It was a short-lived project, with Billy Duffy later forming The Cult. "His first series attempt at doing something was in a group called the nosebleeds, which featured a guitarist by the name of Billy Duffy..."

xref.title: Morrissey's Hero and Name Inspiration
xref.body: Patti Smith, described as a New York poet, was one of Morrissey's heroes. Her name is cited as a possible homage or influence for The Smiths' band name, alongside the deliberate choice for a "plain" name and a Manchester nightclub. "It was also a homage to Patty Smith, the New York poet who was one of Morrissey's heroes..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Morrissey's Inspiration
xref.body: Stephen Patrick Morrissey, who would later become a prominent musician, was a young Manchester poet wannabe and a fan of the New York Dolls. "Still in Manchester, a group soon to be called Joy Division was inspired by a sex pistols show. Many earliest beginnings of the pet shop boys could be traced to what singer Neil Tennant saw and felt at a single pistols concert."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Morrissey's Public Outspokenness
xref.body: Morrissey became highly outspoken about various issues, including animal rights (leading to his "self-righteous vegetarian indignation" on "Meat Is Murder"), Margaret Thatcher's conservative government, the state of music, and the music industry. He was also critical of other stars, making controversial statements about Madonna, reggae music, and even the Live Aid initiative. "This is the record where Morrissey began to be very outspoken about animal rights and meat eaters in general."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Morrissey-Marr Songwriting Alliance
xref.body: The collaboration between Morrissey and Johnny Marr was a "fine, fine songwriting team" that helped reintroduce the pleasures of the two- and three-minute pop song. Their combined talents contributed to Morrissey's lyrical wit, sense of doomed romanticism, and penchant for drama. "While they were together the Morrissey Mar Alliance was a fine, fine songwriting team."

xref.title: Musical Influences
xref.body: All members of The Killers are noted as big fans of The Smiths, Morrissey, The Cure, Blondie, and Duran Duran, drawing inspiration from these artists. "All the guys in the killers are also big fans of the Smiths and Morrissey and the cure and Blondie and Durand-Dorand."

xref.title: Musical Style and Impact
xref.body: The Smiths developed a simple yet distinctive sound featuring guitar, bass, drums, and vocals, blending 1960s rock influences with post-punk aesthetics. Johnny Marr's guitar playing was both fresh and familiar, while Morrissey's lyrics were deep, poetic, and tapped into profound emotional sensitivities. Morrissey's antagonistic persona often generated attention in the music press. The band stood as a counterpoint to the synthesizer and drum machine-dominated music of the early 1980s, creating foundational sounds for future indie eras like Madchester in the late 80s/early 90s and Britpop throughout the rest of the 90s. They are considered the most important British band of the 1980s and the most important indie band the UK and alternative rock have ever produced. "As a package, the Smiths were a pushback against the synthesizers and drum machines that dominated the early part of the 1980s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 2

xref.title: Musical Style and Media Appeal
xref.body: The Smiths, a Manchester band, provided a stark contrast to prevailing trends in British music by emphasizing guitars, bass, drums, and especially lyrics, deliberately avoiding synthesizers. Their sound was built on a solid rhythm section and guitarist Johnny Marr's exceptional songcraft, complemented by singer Morrissey's charisma, personality, and knack for pithy, outrageous quotes, which appealed strongly to the British music media. "The Smiths were exactly the opposite of what was happening in British music at the time. They were all about guitars and bass and drums and lyrics, especially lyrics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: New York Dolls Fan Club Founder
xref.body: As a child, Stephen Patrick Morrissey, the singer for The Smiths, was a fervent fan of the original New York Dolls, writing letters to British music magazines to laud them and founding their British fan club. "In fact, when Morrissey was a kid, he used to write letters to the editors of various British music magazines praising the glories of the original New York dolls. He was even the founder of their British fan club."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

xref.title: Petty Feud with Morrissey (The Smiths)
xref.body: A perceived feud between Robert Smith and Morrissey began in the 1980s, largely perpetuated by the British music media. Morrissey reportedly called Smith a "Wingebag" in an interview, to which Smith retaliated by saying Morrissey was "so depressing that if he doesn't off himself soon, I probably will." Robert Smith later expressed regret for the "petty feud." "Morrissey appears to have started it off by calling Robert Smith a Wingebag in an interview. Smith retaliated in another interview saying that, Morrissey so depressing that if he doesn't off himself soon, I probably will."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Petty Feud with Robert Smith (The Cure)
xref.body: Morrissey initiated a perceived feud in the 1980s by calling Robert Smith a "Wingebag" in an interview, leading to retaliatory remarks from Smith. Morrissey later acknowledged the feud as "petty" and expressed regret. "Morrissey appears to have started it off by calling Robert Smith a Wingebag in an interview."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Smiths Careers and Lawsuit
xref.body: After The Smiths disbanded, Mike Joyce played with bands like Badly Drawn Boy and Suede. Andy Rourke worked as a hired gun before reuniting with Mike in Vinnie Peculiar. In 1996, both sued Morrissey and Marr for non-payment of royalties. Andy settled for £80,000, while Mike was awarded £1.2 million, which Morrissey has continually appealed. "In 1996, both of them sued Morrissey and Mar for non-payment of royalties."

xref.title: Recommended Books
xref.body: Two essential books for understanding The Smiths are "Morrissey and Marr, the severed alliance" by Johnny Rogan, and "The Smiths, songs that saved your life" by Simon Goddard. "If you're a fan, you will love it. If you're not a fan, stay away."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Resolved Conflict and Apology
xref.body: In 2019, Morrissey apologized for his past remarks, claiming they were made 35 years prior and he "didn't mean them," facetiously blaming Tourette's syndrome. Robert Smith responded that the apology was "slightly odd" as the feud had not been at the forefront of his mind for 20-30 years, and he never fully understood the problem to begin with, considering it far from important now. "In 2019, Morrissey said, I said some terrible things about him 35 years ago, but I didn't mean them. It's great when you complain everything on Tourette's syndrome."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Session Player Success, Limited Solo Success
xref.body: As a songwriting partner to Morrissey in The Smiths, Johnny Marr has had a "terrific career as a session player" since the band's breakup. However, his career as a "strictly solo dude" has been less successful, not matching Morrissey's solo trajectory. "He's had a terrific career as a session player, but as a solo dude, like a strictly solo dude, not so much."

xref.title: Unique Musical Style and Thematic Content
xref.body: In 1983, The Smiths distinguished themselves from the dominant heavy hard rock and synthesizer dance music. Their sound was jangly pop with roots in 1950s and 60s music, featuring simple, stark arrangements without big solos or excessive overdubs. Morrissey's vocal style was a croon, likened to Bing Crosby, and his lyrics explored taboo subjects like homosexuality, child molestation, and murder, alongside life and love, but with a unique sense of doomed romanticism and emotional agony. "The Smiths were neither. The music was jangly pop with its roots clearly in the 50s and 60s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Smiths

xref.title: Unique Rhythm Section Dynamic
xref.body: The rhythm section of Mike Joyce on drums and Andy Rourke on bass contributed significantly to The Smiths' unique sound, despite the glory often going to Morrissey and Johnny Marr. Mike Joyce admitted to being a "ham-fisted" player focused on power and volume, while Andy Rourke was known for his funk and subtlety. "As Mike puts it, we had a weird kind of communion."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Unlikely Reunion
xref.body: A reunion of The Smiths is deemed unlikely due to significant bad blood among Morrissey, Johnny Marr, and the other band members. An "ugly court battle" resulted in Morrissey having to pay one million pounds in back royalties to other members. Morrissey also claims no promoter has ever made a big money offer for a reunion tour. "Will there ever be a Smith reunion? Unlikely given that there's a lot of bad blood between Morrissey Johnny Mar and the rest of the band, there was a ugly court battle that resulted in Morrissey having to pay out one million pounds in back royalties to other members of the band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Smiths

xref.title: Visual and Performance Aesthetic
xref.body: During live gigs, The Smiths often featured a gay go-go dancer. Morrissey surrounded himself with fresh flowers and sometimes wore a clunky 1950s-era hearing aid for aesthetic effect, contributing to the band's distinctive image. "Their live gigs featured a gay gogo dancer. Morrissey surrounded himself with fresh flowers, and he often wore a clunky 50s-era hearing aid for some kind of aesthetic effect."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Smiths

xref.title: Whitewashed from Rock History and Posthumous Recognition
xref.body: For a long time, Gerbrieth's existence was "basically whitewashed from rock history." It is only recently, thanks to a dedicated group of fans (including Morrissey) who discovered him after his death, that he is beginning to receive acknowledgment for his significant contributions to music. "for a long, long time, his existence was basically whitewashed from rock history."
